summary: Specifies version 1.3 of Datagram Transport Layer Security, which lets applications communicate over datagram transports while preventing eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery. It is based on TLS 1.3 and gives equivalent security guarantees, except for protection against reordering or replay of messages. It obsoletes RFC 6347.

plainLanguage.summary: DTLS 1.3 protects communication over datagram transports such as UDP. It adapts the TLS 1.3 handshake so it can handle lost, reordered, or repeated packets, but it does not guarantee application data arrives in order or only once.

questions: how does dtls handle packet loss
what is the dtls cookie exchange
subtitle: TLS 1.3 security adapted to transports that can lose, reorder, or duplicate datagrams.

tldr.problem: TLS expects a reliable, ordered transport, while datagram transports can lose, reorder, or duplicate messages. Applications still need protection against eavesdropping, tampering, and forgery.
tldr.mechanism: DTLS 1.3 adapts the TLS 1.3 handshake and record protection with record sequence numbers and epochs, fragmented handshake messages, retransmission timers, ACKs, and an optional cookie exchange for address validation.
tldr.outcome: DTLS 1.3 provides TLS 1.3-equivalent security except for order protection and guaranteed replay protection. RFC 9147 obsoletes RFC 6347 and has been updated by RFC 9853.

today: RFC 9147 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6347 and has been updated by RFC 9853.

sections.title: Why TLS Needs Changes for Datagrams
sections.content:
TLS establishes an authenticated channel that protects confidentiality and integrity, but it normally runs over a reliable transport such as TCP. DTLS brings similar communication security to datagram transports and is designed to stay close to TLS so implementations can reuse code and infrastructure.

Datagram transport does not promise reliable or in-order delivery. DTLS preserves that behavior for application data; it does not recover lost application data or reorder it. The protocol adds sequence numbers for records, sequence numbers and fragmentation fields for handshake messages, and a return-routability check to address denial-of-service risks.

DTLS 1.3 is based on TLS 1.3 and obsoletes DTLS 1.2. The RFC says there is no DTLS 1.1 because the version number was skipped to align DTLS numbering with TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS protects data on a transport that may lose or reorder packets. It adds recovery for the handshake, but leaves delivery of application data to the underlying transport.

sections.title: Records, Headers, and Epochs
sections.content:
DTLS sends unprotected records as DTLSPlaintext and protected records as DTLSCiphertext. The protected form uses a variable-length unified header. Its first three bits are 001; other bits indicate whether a Connection ID and length are present, the sequence-number length, and the low bits of the epoch.

An epoch identifies a set of keys. Record sequence numbers restart at zero for each epoch. Protected records encrypt the sequence number, using a mask derived from the ciphertext. If the unified header omits its length, that record MUST be the last record in the datagram. Each record must fit in one datagram, although a datagram may contain multiple records.

For demultiplexing, alert, handshake, and ACK content types are plaintext. Other records whose leading bits are 001 are processed as ciphertext; other values are rejected. The RFC reserves content type values 32 through 63 to support this distinction.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protected record indicates which key period to use and carries a partly hidden sequence number. A record stays within one datagram, and the receiver uses the header to identify its type and boundaries.

sections.title: The Handshake, Address Check, and Fragments
sections.content:
DTLS 1.3 reuses the TLS 1.3 handshake messages and flow, with changes for loss, reordering, and fragmentation. Handshake headers add a message sequence number, fragment offset, and fragment length. A receiver can queue messages that arrive before earlier messages and reassemble fragments.

A server may reply to a ClientHello with a HelloRetryRequest carrying a stateless cookie. The client sends another ClientHello with that cookie; the server proceeds only if it validates. This checks that the client can receive packets at its apparent address and makes denial-of-service attacks using forged source addresses more difficult. It does not protect against attacks from valid addresses. Servers SHOULD perform the cookie exchange by default, and clients MUST be prepared for it on every handshake.

A DTLS record must fit in one datagram. A large handshake message can be divided among records, each with fragment offset and length fields. The fragments can be reassembled without relying on IP fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Handshake messages have sequence and fragment information so the peers can handle missing or out-of-order pieces. A cookie exchange checks that the client can receive data at the address it used.

sections.title: Flights, Timers, and Acknowledgements
sections.content:
A handshake groups messages into flights: one peer sends a flight, then expects a response. The retransmission state machine moves through PREPARING, SENDING, WAITING, and FINISHED. If a timer expires, the sender retransmits unacknowledged messages.

Unless deployment information gives a better estimate, implementations SHOULD start with a retransmission timer of 1000 ms and double it each time, up to no less than 60 seconds. DTLS-SRTP is given a recommended default of 400 ms. Because DTLS has no built-in congestion control, stacks SHOULD NOT send more than 10 records in one transmission.

The ACK content type is 26. An ACK lists handshake records received and processed or buffered. It can prompt selective retransmission before the timer expires. ACKs are required for flights that have no implicit acknowledgement, including the client's final handshake flight and post-handshake messages such as NewSessionTicket.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers group handshake messages into flights and resend messages that have not been acknowledged. ACKs identify received records so a peer can resend only the missing parts.

sections.title: Key Changes and Connection IDs
sections.content:
An endpoint sends KeyUpdate when it changes its sending keys. The other endpoint must acknowledge the update. The sender must wait for that ACK before sending with the new keys or sending another KeyUpdate; the receiver retains old keys until it successfully decrypts a message using the new keys. Each key change advances the epoch.

If the peers negotiated Connection IDs, they can send NewConnectionId messages and request additional identifiers with RequestConnectionId. A new identifier can be used when sending over a new path. The RFC says fresh identifiers can improve privacy across paths, and sequence-number encryption also makes simple tracking harder.

DTLS 1.3 uses the key-derivation label prefix dtls13, separating its keys from TLS 1.3 keys. A sender MUST NOT allow the epoch to exceed 2^48-1.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers confirm a key update before the sender uses its new keys. If they negotiated connection identifiers, they can change those identifiers when network paths change.

sections.title: Application Data
sections.content:
Application data travels in records protected with the current connection state. The record layer treats application messages as data to carry, splitting them into records as needed.

DTLS preserves datagram behavior for this data. An application using DTLS must account for packets that may be lost, duplicated, or delivered out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS protects application data in records, but does not make the transport reliable. Applications still need to handle missing or reordered data when that matters.

sections.title: Security Guarantees and Limits
sections.content:
Except for order protection and non-replayability, DTLS 1.3 has the same security guarantees as TLS 1.3. DTLS does not provide order protection and may not provide replay protection; its per-record replay check is optional. Invalid records SHOULD usually be silently discarded rather than terminating the association.

Because invalid records can be ignored, an attacker may make repeated forgery attempts. Implementations MUST count authentication failures for each key and apply limits for the negotiated AEAD algorithm. The RFC sets a limit of 2^36 failed records for AEAD_AES_128_GCM, AEAD_AES_256_GCM, and AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305. TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 MUST NOT be used without additional safeguards against forgery.

The cookie exchange helps prevent resource-exhaustion and amplification attacks using forged client addresses, but does not stop attacks from valid addresses. A server should rotate its cookie secret. Connection ID address changes also need a reachability test; this RFC does not define that test.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS protects records but does not guarantee their order or always prevent replay. Servers also need safeguards for repeated invalid records and for requests from unverified addresses.
